cells.title: Understand the problem and the design tree
cells.task:
First understand what the item's `background` asks for, only as far as you need to know where in the design tree to
look. Then read the tree for it as the tree's rules say. The research comes next, in this session, and starts from
what you read here: this run is for the tree of this repository, `design/`, and whatever else the `background` names
is read in the research. What you read stays in this session for the research: hand in only `dealt_with`.

cells.title: Initial research
cells.task:
Research how to do what the item asks with code, going on from the tree you read. Check that what the item says
holds, where it shows: a fault it reports, seen as it happens, such as on the page in a real browser or in the
program on its own data, and its root cause (a cause read from the code, or a test in a stand-in such as a simulated
page, has not seen it); what it asks for, not there already. Where it does not hold after looking as far as the tools
reach, ask the owner how to go on, with a question that waits. A test goes with the project's tests, anything else you
make in `project.research`, committed. If the design itself is at fault, say so.

Decide `deep_needed`. With yes, write only `found`. With no, write the plan (`plan_owner`, `plan_agent`,
`acceptance`, and `tree_edits`) and no `found`. Where the solution needs the design tree changed, propose that in
`tree_edits` rather than bend the solution. Before handing in, ask yourself where the plan is most likely wrong, and
check that point.

cells.title: Is there a better way
cells.task:
Think it through again from first principles: what does what `background` asks need at bottom, and does the plan make
sense for it? Is there a better way: the same end by another way, more simply, at less running cost or with less to
keep up, with a better structure in the code, more complete in what it should cover, truer to the project's intent; a
way a decision of the tree rules out included. Think again in earnest; do not answer for the sake of answering.

If there is, write the plan again for it, changed only where the better way changes it; where it needs the design tree
changed, propose that in `tree_edits`. If not, change nothing.

cells.title: Deep research
cells.task:
Research what `found` left open, and work out how to do what `background` asks. This session has not read the tree:
read it for the work as the tree's rules say, and the code yourself. Take `found` as a hypothesis to verify, and use
what the research left in `project.research` rather than run it again; anything you make goes there too, committed.
Find out a fact left open, try the ways to try, analyse a fault of the design itself as a design; verify a fact that
would change the direction before using it, and weigh the upkeep the solution adds.

Write the plan: `plan_owner`, `plan_agent`, `acceptance`, and `tree_edits`. In `plan_owner` say also
what it leaves out. Where the solution needs the design tree changed, propose that in `tree_edits` rather than bend
the solution. Settle what a fact settles and decide what is cheap to change later, and ask the owner the rest.

If the solution falls into parts each mergeable on its own, too large for one work, ask the owner with a question
that waits, naming them in order.

cells.title: Design review
cells.task:
You review the plan in a session of your own: you did not write it, so look for what its writer cannot see. Where
this session has not yet read the tree for this item, first understand what `background` asks, then read the tree for
it as the tree's rules say, and the code the plan changes. The plan is `plan_owner`, `plan_agent`, `acceptance` and
`tree_edits`, with the questions its writer asked the owner.

Judge it only by what it was made for (what `background` asks) and the repository's rules, on each of these points:
1. Whether it does what `background` asks, no less and no more, and, where there was deep research, settles what
   `found` left to it.
2. Its design by the engineering rules: the responsibilities, interfaces and representations it touches, one place
   for each thing, nothing that no current work needs.
3. The acceptance: whether each condition can be decided, a wrong result would fail it, and together they cover what
   `background` asks.
4. The questions: a question a fact could settle or that is cheap to change later; a choice only the owner can make
   that no question asks; a question not marked in `plan_owner`.

In the why of `plan_ok`, answer each point by its number: none, or what you found. Write what the writer must take in
`plan_review`, every point at once: this is your one chance, and nothing is raised later that could be raised now.
With `plan_ok` yes, leave `plan_review` out of your return. Leave out what you are not sure is better.

watches.name: plan
watches.do: See what changed in the plan since the version you last reviewed, the whole of it where you reviewed none, and review it.

watches.name: plan_review
watches.do: Where the writer answered an earlier point in `plan_review`, accept the answer or say why not; never raise a point again without saying so, and raise nothing new the answers did not bring.

cells.title: Design tree review
cells.task:
You review the plan against the design tree, in a session that did not write it. Where this session has not yet read
the tree for this item, first understand what `background` asks, then read the tree for it as the tree's rules say, and
the code the plan changes. The plan is `plan_owner`, `plan_agent`, `acceptance` and `tree_edits`, with the questions
its writer asked the owner.

Judge it by the tree's rules, on each of these points:
1. What it goes against: an article of the constitution, a principle, a decision, or a design document, which may be
   ahead of the code: the plan builds toward it, never away from it.
2. What its change makes untrue: each entry that will no longer say what the code does, which `tree_edits` must
   rewrite or delete.
3. What it leaves out: a way it weighed and turned down, something done on purpose that would look like a fault, a
   relation between two places that neither shows, or a rule later works must follow, which no entry records.
4. Each entry of `tree_edits`, as one that must earn its place: its kind and its concept in the tree, whether its
   reason is the real one, an entry it contradicts or repeats, its form, and whether it says what this plan builds and
   no more.
5. A change of the tree in `tree_edits`, of the constitution, a principle, a decision or a document, that no
   question asks the owner about.

In the why of `tree_ok`, answer each point by its number: none, or what you found. Write what the writer must take in
`tree_review`, every point at once: this is your one chance, and nothing is raised later that could be raised now.
With `tree_ok` yes, leave `tree_review` out of your return. Leave out what you are not sure is better.

watches.name: tree_review

cells.title: Implement
cells.task:
Implement `plan_agent`, changing only what this work needs. Follow for each question put to the owner the option the
owner took, or else the one it recommends, and write into `design/` what `tree_edits` holds: an entry may follow
main's tree in wording and place, not in meaning. Start from a test that shows what the change is for, red on the code
before it: the research's, where it left one. Run each test you add or extend on the change and on the code before it;
a test removed, skipped or weakened needs a technical reason. Where cost per operation or request can change, measure
what it can make slower as well as what it is for.

Where the plan does not hold (its direction is wrong, or it needs a tree decision changed or a choice the owner has
not made, such as accepting a slowdown), do not work around it: say where and why in `plan_doubts`; the
answer comes there too: judge it, and write `plan_doubts` again only where a doubt still stands.

Commit everything in the worktree, and hand in `code`, `decisions` and `evidence` once the project's check passes on
your last commit: `title` with your first `code` and again when what the change does changes, `decisions` only where
there is one, and `acceptance` only when a condition must change, the whole list as it now stands, with why.

Where main does not merge into the branch, merge it in yourself and run the check again. A point its judge insists on,
fix or have the owner rule. If what the item asks needs no change, ask the owner.

cells.title: Review
cells.task:
Review the change in `code`, in a session of your own, and change no file. Read the diff from main to `head`, and
whole each file of decisions whose topic it touches. Judge only by what the implementation
was asked to do (`plan_owner`, `acceptance`) and the repository's rules.

Does the code do what the plan says, to the standard the tree sets? The work is done once it does; old code that lagged
behind a decision before this work is no point. A short cut, another method, more than the work needs or a change of
direction is a point; so is code that breaks a decision of the tree, or a decision that neither the plan nor the tree
records and `decisions` does not give a reason that holds for. Is it sound in structure and lines? Does the change reach
every place where the same thing happens, not only the one the item names? Does `evidence` show each condition on the
change, each new test red before the change where its kind needs it and worth its time? Is each exception or expected
value the change gives a check a choice of the design, not a fault it hides? Where cost per operation can change, is
what it can slow measured? Do the entries written into `design/` say what `tree_edits` says, and no more? Is each
change of a file the project protects one the work needs?

List every point at once in `review`: this is your one chance, and nothing is raised later that could be raised now.
Leave out preferences: the engineer fixes nearly all a review raises, so a wrong point makes good code worse.

With `review_ok` yes, leave `review` out of your return. Having said yes to `needs_testing`, keep it while the part of
the change that made you say so is still there.

watches.name: change
watches.do: See what changed since the version you last reviewed, the whole of it where you reviewed none, and review it.

watches.name: review
watches.do: Look at what changed: accept each answer in `review` or say why not; raise nothing new the fix did not bring.

cells.title: Adversarial testing
cells.task:
Test the change in `code` in a session of your own, looking for where it is wrong. You only write tests, in the
project's test files: where you think the implementation wrong, write a test that turns red, for the engineer to fix.
Meet each condition of `acceptance` that a test can show by a test, the engineer's where it really tests it, else
yours; then dig for corner cases. Each test of yours names the independent reference its verdict rests on, such as a
specification or an established implementation; what you think should hold does not count. A new-behaviour test fails
before the change; an old-behaviour test passes before and after. Run every test new in this work on the change and
on the code before it; one of yours whose result before misfits its kind, fix and run again now,
and one of the engineer's, say so in `testing`. One red
after the change, check against its reference first; hand on only what stays red. Commit your tests on the work's
branch.

Hand in `tests`, and what stays red or stays suspect in `testing`, every point at once: this is your one chance, and
nothing is raised later that could be raised now. With `testing_ok` yes, leave `testing` out of your return.

watches.name: testing
watches.do: Run your tests on the new commit: accept each answer in `testing`, checking a test called wrong against its reference, or say why not.
